problem: The answer says the tube is 'blind for the whole second' while also recording about 5000 counts in that second. A dead-time fraction of 1.0 does not mean zero output; it means the observed rate has reached its ceiling of 1/τ = 1/(200 µs) = 5000 counts per second, so the tube is dead between pulses but still emits the maximum possible number of pulses. As written, a student will read the two statements as contradicting each other.
fix: Dead-time fraction = observed rate × dead time = 5000 s⁻¹ × 200 × 10⁻⁶ s = 1.0. The tube can never deliver more than 1/τ = 5000 counts per second, so at this rate it is saturated: it is dead between pulses and the true rate is much higher than 5000 per second. Dilute the sample or apply a dead-time correction.

problem: 'only the scintillation counter does that' overstates the case: proportional counters and semiconductor detectors (for example cadmium zinc telluride, mentioned in the Beyond section) also give pulse heights that follow the radiation energy.
fix: The GM pulse height does not give the radiation energy; energy information comes from detectors whose pulse height follows the deposited energy, such as the scintillation counter, the proportional counter or a semiconductor detector.

problem: Absorbed dose is defined as energy deposited per kilogram of tissue. The gray is defined for any material, not only tissue; radiation dosimetry applies it to tissue, but the definition should not be tied to tissue.
fix: Absorbed dose is the energy deposited per kilogram of the material absorbing it, measured in gray (Gy): 1 Gy = 1 J/kg.

problem: The answer defines the sievert as 'equivalent dose', which just repeats the name of the quantity instead of defining the unit.
fix: 1 Sv is the equivalent dose when the absorbed dose in Gy is multiplied by the radiation weighting factor (1 for gamma rays, so 1 Gy gives 1 Sv); numerically 1 Sv = 1 J/kg for gamma rays.
